newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Retailer Somerfield boosts profits. [CORRECTED 14:31 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Retailer Somerfield boosts profits. [CORRECTED 14:31 GMT]

text.p: British food retailer Somerfield Plc said on Tuesday there had been marked improvement in its performance, paving the way for future expansion, as it unveiled its first results since flotation last August.
In an interview finance director Martin Gatto said the improvement was partly achieved by increased sales of higher margin fresh foods, such as delicatessan, fish and bakery.
"Those are high margin departments...and the effect of that is to give you a better margin," he told Reuters.

Pretax profit in the 28 weeks to November 9, 1996 were 54.6 million pounds ($90.68 million), up from 43.0 million while sales rose 1.3 percent to 1.71 billion pounds from 1.69 billion. The company said its sales in comparable store space rose four percent in the first nine weeks of the second half.
But Somerfield shares fell 5p to 169p in early trade as some brokers saw investors, who had bought the shares at their August flotation price of 145 pence, take profits.
"Maybe it was better to travel than arrive, but people who bought at 150p and rode it up have got a nice return," said David Stoddart, analyst at Henderson Crosthwaite.
Analysts' expectations for Somerfield profits were in a range between 52.5 million and 56 million pounds.

"But given that the background in the industry is no worse than it has been for a while it is hard to see why Somerfield should suffer particularly," Stoddart said. "Refurbishments are still producing good returns and there is more to come, and the stock is not expensive however you measure it."
Improved buying terms as well as strong fresh food sales helped drive an increase of one percentage point in gross margin in the first half.
"We've improved our operating ratios in a very competitive market," said Gatto, "And improved our gross margin when most others in the industry are seeing their margin decline."
The group held its position as the fifth biggest British food retailer with a market share of about 5.3 percent, behind Tesco Plc, J. Sainsbury Plc, Safeway Plc and ASDA Group Plc.
Gatto said he expected the food retail market to remain highly competitive, but did not see a new price war looming.

The group, created in one of the big leveraged-buyouts of the 1980s, is in the process of converting its old Gateway stores into the new-style Somerfield format and has so far converted 74 percent of its selling space.
It has converted 424 stores, leaving 150 Gateways and plans to convert about 110 of these and sell or close 30 or 40 of them over the next three or four years.
Gatto said the group planned to open seven new stores in 1997/98 (corrects to delete reference to 100,000 square foot stores).
Somerfield is also experimenting with petrol station shops and has opened one already in association with Elf Aquitaine.

Sales in Somerfield stores in the half year were up 4.3 percent, while sales in the unconverted shops fell 5.5 percent. Its Food Giant stores suffered a six percent drop in sales, which the group said was disappointing.
The retailer proposed a dividend of 3.4 pence. ($1=.6021 Pound)
